title: The honey Dadhyanch risked his head for
hookLine: a sage with a horse's head teaches the honey: everything feeds everything
carry: madhu: all feeds all, one self in each
tomorrow: what do a teacher and a student say before a hard lesson?

lines: TEACH IT AND LOSE YOUR HEAD.
A HORSE'S HEAD, A SECRET TOLD.
cards: Some secrets cost a head. In an old Vedic story, the sage Dadhyanch knows a secret teaching, and the god Indra warns him: teach it to anyone and your head comes off. The twin healer gods, the Ashvins, want it anyway.
So they give Dadhyanch a horse's head, and he teaches them through it. Indra strikes it off, and the Ashvins put the sage's own head back on. The secret was called the honey.
The Brihadaranyaka tells us what it said.

teach.b: The passage is called the honey teaching, madhu. It goes around the world one thing at a time. This earth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this earth.
The waters, the same. Fire, wind, the sun, the sky, the moon, lightning, thunder: each one honey for all beings, and all beings honey for it. Nothing here only gives or only takes.
And in each one, the text says, there is a shining, deathless person, and the same shining person within the body. That one is the self. Then the close: this self is Brahman, the experiencer of all.
That's the honey Dadhyanch risked his head for, and it's a core Hindu teaching: the world isn't a pile of separate things using each other up. It's one web, and the same self shines in every strand.
And with it, a set is complete.

teach.h: FOUR SAYINGS, ONE FROM EACH VEDA.
teach.b: Tradition gathers four great sayings, one from the Upanishads of each Veda: prajnanam brahma, from the Aitareya; aham brahmasmi, from the Brihadaranyaka; tat tvam asi, from the Chandogya; and ayam atma brahma, from the Mandukya.
Each Vedanta school reads them in its own way, and now all four have had their turn.

how: Students of the Brihadaranyaka read the honey teaching (2.5) as one long passage, and teachers often present the four mahavakyas together, one from the Upanishads of each Veda, at the end of studying them.

o: this self is Brahman, in all that feeds and is fed
honey offered to the gods on a temple altar
a blessing said over food before a big feast

games.q: four great sayings, four Upanishads. tap the pairs.

s: in the honey teaching, people take and the earth gives
earth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for the earth: everything feeds and is fed.
the honey teaching ends on 'this self is Brahman'
Brihadaranyaka 2.5.19: this self is Brahman, the experiencer of all.
in the story, the Ashvins gave Dadhyanch a horse's head so he could teach them the honey
Indra cut it off, and the Ashvins restored the sage's own head; the Brihadaranyaka points to the story at 2.5.16–17.

games.q: you're cooking with your grandmother. she thanks the vegetables, the farmer, and then you, for chopping. by the honey teaching, why you too?
o: just politeness; only the food is the real gift here.
she's practicing thanking everyone so no one feels left out.
you're part of what feeds and is fed, like everything else.
games.why: in the honey teaching nothing only gives or only takes. the earth feeds you, and you are honey for the earth too.

practice: If there's honey near you, or anything sweet, take a little and let it rest on your tongue before you swallow. Trace it back: the flower, the rain, the ground, the hands that carried it to you.
If there's nothing to taste, breathe in slowly and notice the air feeding you, and your breath warming it in return.

wordCard.voice: Ayam atma brahma, the honey way: everything feeds and is fed, and in each, the same shining self. The last day with this saying.

orig.note: Sanskrit: honey; the passage at Brihadaranyaka 2.5 is known as the honey teaching.

carryVoice: For the road: everything feeds and is fed, and the same self shines in each. That was the honey Dadhyanch risked his head for. Four sayings, done.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.5.1–19 (the honey teaching; 2.5.19: this self is Brahman, the experiencer of all)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.5.16–17 (this is the honey Dadhyanch Atharvana taught the Ashvins; quoting the Rig Veda: with a horse's head he told you the honey)
Shatapatha Brahmana 14.1.1.18–24 (Indra's threat to behead Dadhyanch; the Ashvins give him a horse's head; it is cut off and his own restored); Rig Veda 1.116.12, 1.117.22
Mandukya Upanishad 2 (ayam atma brahma); Aitareya 3.3, Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10, Chandogya 6.8.7 (the other three sayings)
the traditional grouping of four mahavakyas, one from the Upanishads of each Veda
